items.title: The far-field gradient of a compactly supported Newtonian potential
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the Lebesgue interface used below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge3$, let $\Phi$ be the fundamental solution of $-\Delta$ on $\mathbb R^n$ normalised by $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$ ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]]), so that for $z\ne0$
$$\Phi(z)=\frac{|z|^{2-n}}{(n-2)\omega_{n-1}},\qquad \nabla\Phi(z)=-\frac{z}{\omega_{n-1}|z|^n},\qquad |\nabla\Phi(z)|=\frac{1}{\omega_{n-1}|z|^{n-1}},$$
let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ be real, measurable and zero $\lambda_n$-almost everywhere outside a closed ball $\overline B_R(0)=\{x:|x|\le R\}$ of finite radius $R>0$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), and let
$$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y)$$
be the Newtonian potential ([[def-newtonian-potential]]). Then:
(a) [Representation and differentiability off the far field] for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $|x|>2R$ the integral $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\nabla\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y)$ is absolutely convergent, the function $Nf$ is differentiable at $x$ with
$$\nabla(Nf)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\nabla\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y),$$
and $x\mapsto\nabla(Nf)(x)$ is continuous on the open set $\{x:|x|>2R\}$;
(b) [Decay bound] for every $x$ with $|x|>2R$,
$$|\nabla(Nf)(x)|\le\frac{2^{n-1}\|f\|_1}{\omega_{n-1}|x|^{n-1}},\qquad \|f\|_1:=\int_{\mathbb R^n}|f|\,d\lambda_n;$$
(c) [Scope] the hypothesis is compact support together with $L^1$-integrability; no boundedness of $f$ is assumed, and nothing is asserted at points with $|x|\le2R$ (where the kernel singularity may meet the support of $f$).
items.strategy: Fix $x_0$ with $|x_0|>2R$ and choose $0<\delta<|x_0|-2R$. On the full open ball $U=B_\delta(x_0)$, every $y\in\overline B_R$ obeys $|x-y|\ge |x_0|-\delta-R=:c>0$. Thus both $|\Phi(x-y)f(y)|\le c^{2-n}|f(y)|/((n-2)\omega_{n-1})$ and $|\partial_i\Phi(x-y)f(y)|\le c^{1-n}|f(y)|/\omega_{n-1}$ hold throughout $U$, outside the single null set on which $f$ may fail to vanish off $\overline B_R$. Equivalently reset $f$ to zero on that set without changing any integral. The majorants are integrable; the kernel and its coordinate derivatives are continuous off zero and their products with measurable $f$ are measurable ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Restricting to each sufficiently short coordinate interval through any $x\in U$, [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] yields $\partial_iNf(x)=\int\partial_i\Phi(x-y)f(y)dy$. For any sequence $x_m\to x$ in $U$, the derivative integrands converge almost everywhere and have the same full-neighbourhood majorant $c^{1-n}|f|/\omega_{n-1}$. [[thm-dominated-convergence]] therefore proves continuity of each partial derivative as a function of all coordinates on $U$, not merely along coordinate lines. [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]] now gives total differentiability and the displayed gradient representation; the continuous vector of partials is the gradient ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). As $x_0$ was arbitrary, (a) holds throughout the stated far field. For (b), $|x-y|\ge |x|-R>|x|/2$ on the support, so $|\nabla\Phi(x-y)|\le2^{n-1}/(\omega_{n-1}|x|^{n-1})$; integrating against $|f|$ gives the stated bound. No boundedness of $f$ or interior-support assertion is used. The support ball is measurable, and the choice cost is exactly the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of the measure interfaces.

items.title: The distributional gradient of a locally integrable function smooth off one point
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) for the Lebesgue and product-measure interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $p\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$ be continuous on $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{p\}$ and of class $C^1$ there, with each classical partial derivative $\partial_iu:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{p\}\to\mathbb R$ (extended by $0$ at $p$) again in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$. Then for every $i=1,\dots,n$, with $T_u\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ the regular distribution of $u$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $\partial_i$ the distributional derivative ([[def-distributional-derivative]]),
$$\partial_iT_u=T_{\partial_iu}\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n),$$
that is, $\langle\partial_iT_u,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\partial_iu\,\psi\,d\lambda_n$ for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]). The value assigned to $\partial_iu$ at the single point $p$ is immaterial, because a singleton is Lebesgue null ([[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]], [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). Both hypotheses are used: $u$ must be locally integrable and continuous away from $p$, and each classical partial must be locally integrable; the lemma is asserted for one exceptional point, not for an exceptional set of positive surface measure.
items.strategy:
The given $u$ is continuous off $p$, hence Borel there; assigning a finite value at $p$ makes a Borel representative on all of $\mathbb R^n$. Each classical partial is continuous off $p$ and is extended by zero there, hence is also Borel. Thus the products with tests below are Borel, so the cited Borel product-measure identification applies directly. Fix $i$ and $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$; both $\partial_iu\,\psi$ and $u\,\partial_i\psi$ are integrable on $\mathbb R^n$: for the first, $|\partial_iu\,\psi|\le\|\psi\|_\infty|\partial_iu|$ with $\partial_iu\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and $\psi$ compactly supported, and for the second $|u\,\partial_i\psi|\le\|\partial_i\psi\|_\infty|u|$ with $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Split $\mathbb R^n=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{n-1}$ into the $i$-th coordinate $t$ and the remaining coordinates $y$; identify the Lebesgue measure with the product measure ([[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]], [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]], [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]), so that [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] applies to both integrable functions. Let $Y$ be the set of $y$ for which the line $\{(t,y):t\in\mathbb R\}$ meets $p$: it is the single transverse point $y=p'$, a $\lambda_{n-1}$-null set by [[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]] (this is where $n\ge2$ is used: for $n=1$ there are no transverse coordinates and the case would have to be argued separately by absolute continuity). For every $y\notin Y$ the line misses $p$, so $t\mapsto u(t,y)$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R$ with derivative $t\mapsto\partial_iu(t,y)$, and $t\mapsto u(t,y)\psi(t,y)$ is $C^1$ with compact support; [[thm-integration-by-parts]] (equivalently the fundamental theorem, [[thm-ftc-first-part]]) on an interval containing the support gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R}\partial_iu(t,y)\psi(t,y)\,dt=-\int_{\mathbb R}u(t,y)\partial_i\psi(t,y)\,dt.$$
This holds for every $y\notin Y$, hence almost everywhere. Fubini's theorem applied to the two integrable functions gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\partial_iu\,\psi\,d\lambda_n=\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}\!\!\int_{\mathbb R}(\partial_iu\,\psi)\,dt\,dy=-\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}\!\!\int_{\mathbb R}(u\,\partial_i\psi)\,dt\,dy=-\int_{\mathbb R^n}u\,\partial_i\psi\,d\lambda_n.$$
The right-hand side is $-\langle T_u,\partial_i\psi\rangle=\langle\partial_iT_u,\psi\rangle$ by the definition of the distributional derivative ([[def-distribution]]), and the left-hand side is $\langle T_{\partial_iu},\psi\rangle$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]). Hence $\partial_iT_u=T_{\partial_iu}$. Measurability of $\partial_iu$ is not assumed beyond the stated $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ membership of its extension: on $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{p\}$ it is the pointwise limit of the difference quotients of the measurable $u$, hence measurable there by the closure properties of measurable functions ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and the single point $p$ does not affect the classes ([[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The splitting, the identification of the product measure and the two Fubini applications are the only measure-theoretic inputs; the choice cost is the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Finite-interval integrations of the continuous one-variable test/radial integrands above use [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]] to identify their Riemann/FTC values with their Lebesgue values before Fubini, polar integration or passage to improper limits; real and imaginary test components are treated separately.

items.title: Euclidean balls, annuli and spheres as bounded smooth domains and hypersurfaces
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the boundary-chart and surface-measure interfaces used below ([[def-countable-choice]]). On $\mathbb R^3$ with its Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]) let $0<\varepsilon<R$ and put
$$B_R:=\{x:|x|<R\},\qquad \overline B_R:=\{x:|x|\le R\},\qquad A_{\varepsilon,R}:=\{x:\varepsilon<|x|<R\},\qquad S_r:=\{x:|x|=r\}.$$
Then:
(a) [Domains] $B_R$ and $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ are bounded $C^1$ domains in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; their boundaries are $S_R$, respectively $S_\varepsilon\cup S_R$, and the corresponding outward unit normals are
$$\nu(x)=\frac{x}{|x|}\ \ (x\in S_R),\qquad \nu(x)=-\frac{x}{|x|}\ \ (x\in S_\varepsilon,\ \text{boundary of }A_{\varepsilon,R});$$
(b) [Spheres] each $S_r$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ (indeed $C^\infty$) hypersurface in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] with two-sided unit normals $\pm x/|x|$, and the closed annulus $\overline A_{\varepsilon,R}$ together with the faces $S_\varepsilon,S_R$ and the empty edge set is a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ in the sense of [[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]];
(c) [Consequences used downstream] the divergence theorem and Green's first identity of [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]] and [[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] apply on $B_R$ and on $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ with the outward normals of (a), and $S_r$ carries a finite Borel surface measure with the standard graph charts.
items.strategy: The continuous norm makes $B_R$ and $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ nonempty bounded open sets, and radial perturbations show their boundaries are respectively $S_R$ and $S_\varepsilon\cup S_R$ ([[thm-continuity-preimage-characterisation]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]). Here is an explicit finite graph cover of a sphere $S_r$. For $k=1,2,3$ and $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$ use the relatively open patch $\sigma x_k>r/(2\sqrt3)$; these six patches cover because some $|x_k|\ge r/\sqrt3$. In rigid coordinates $(y,z)$ with $z=\sigma x_k$, each patch lies on the positive graph $z=h(y)=\sqrt{r^2-|y|^2}$. Around each point choose a graph cylinder small enough that $z>0$, $|y|<r$ and any other annulus boundary is absent. The sphere is exactly this graph, and the ball is exactly $z<h(y)$ there. In particular reflection of a lower physical hemisphere yields the positive graph $+\sqrt{r^2-|y|^2}$, not the negative graph. The chain and power rules make $h$ smooth on $|y|<r$ ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]). For the inner boundary of the annulus the domain is locally the complement of $\overline B_\varepsilon$. Starting with $z=\sigma x_k>0$, reflect once more to $w=-z$; the graph is $w=-h(y)$ and the exterior condition $z>h(y)$ becomes exactly the required subgraph $w<-h(y)$. The outer boundary uses the ball chart. The definition's graph normal $(-Dh,1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$, with $Dh=-y/h$, transports to $x/r$ for the ball/outer sphere. For the complement chart $g=-h$, its graph normal is $(-Dg,1)/\sqrt{1+|Dg|^2}=(-y,h)/r$ in $(y,w)$; transport by $w=-\sigma x_k$ gives $-x/r$, the annulus inner normal. Hence (a) and its signs follow from [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Each sphere is closed and bounded, hence compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], and the six smooth graph patches make it a compact embedded smooth hypersurface with two-sided normals. The annulus has the two compact faces $S_\varepsilon,S_R$, empty edge set, and the normals just computed, so it is a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation ([[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]). The divergence theorem and first Green identity apply to these domains with precisely those normals ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]], [[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]). The compact chart surface carries finite Borel measure by [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. The only choice cost is the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of that interface.

items.title: The static and pure electrostatic regimes and their fixed-time reading
items.statement:
Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units, constants and symbols of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and let $(\rho,J)$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$, all of class $C^1$ (with every additional derivative appearing below existing and continuous); $\partial_t$ is the partial time derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].
(a) [Static regime] The **static (time-independent) electromagnetic regime** on $\Omega\times I$ is the requirement
$$\partial_tE=0,\qquad\partial_tB=0,\qquad\partial_t\rho=0,\qquad\partial_tJ=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$
(b) [Pure electrostatics] The **pure electrostatic regime** is the static regime together with $J=0$ and $B=0$ on $\Omega\times I$.
(c) [Reduced equations] If the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds in the static regime, then the four Maxwell equations reduce to
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$$
pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied at each fixed time; in the pure electrostatic regime the reduction is exactly the pair $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$.
(d) [Fixed-time reading] In the static regime $E,B,\rho,J$ do not depend on $t$, so each is the pullback along $(y,t)\mapsto y$ of a single map on $\Omega$; this fixed-time reading (the spatial field or source) is the object analysed by the electrostatic statements of this page, and no other time dependence is introduced. The equations of (c) are equations between those spatial maps.
(e) [Static-to-distributional reading] Let fields $E,B$ and volume densities $\rho,J$ be locally integrable and time independent on $\Omega\times I$, and let $\Omega$ be open. Then, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the cited measure and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), the weak equations of the solution predicate of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e) for these time-independent objects hold if and only if the four spatial equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$; the passage between them is the integration in $t$ of the pairings against $C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ tests, justified by [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] after identifying fields and densities with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). In particular a **stationary point charge** at $x_0\in\Omega$ with charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ is the point source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with constant trajectory $z(t)\equiv x_0$, whose pairing is $\psi\mapsto q\int_I\psi(x_0,t)\,dt$ and whose fixed-time reading is the spatial point source $\eta\mapsto q\eta(x_0)$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).
(f) [Conventions and scope] The regime is imposed in the one inertial frame of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; no claim is made that time independence survives a change of inertial description, and where a frame change is used the transformed fields must be rechecked. The static regime is an adopted idealization, not a dynamical stability theorem: static charged matter requires external support or an adopted equilibrium model. No equation is asserted here for singular sources beyond the dictionary of (e), and no empirical claim is made.
items.strategy: For the locally integrable branch use Borel representatives of each spatial component, obtained under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ from [[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]] and [[thm-completion-measurable-functions-have-base-measurable-representatives]] after zero extension outside $\Omega$. These changes are on spatial null sets and their products with compact time intervals are null, so they do not change spatial or spacetime regular distributions. With [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]] and [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]], the pairings may therefore be evaluated using the product measure and Fubini below. A convention definition with the two elementary verifications (c) and (e). For (c): substituting $\partial_tE=\partial_tB=0$ into $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ of the smooth branch ([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]) gives $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ at each fixed time, while $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $\operatorname{div}B=0$ are the unchanged divergence equations; the identification of the operators at fixed time is that of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], applied to the fixed-time fields of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]]. In the pure case $B=0$, $J=0$ this pair reads $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$, which are identities. For (d): time independence makes $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ the composition of $(y,t)\mapsto y$ with $y\mapsto F(y,t_0)$ for any fixed $t_0$; that the fixed-time value is independent of $t_0$ uses only the vanishing of all the $\partial_t$'s and the differentiability convention of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] (a $C^1$ function on the interval $I$ with zero derivative is constant, cf. the mean-value theorem for the single variable $t$). For (e): write the four pairings of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e) with $\psi\in C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$; for each fixed $t$ the map $\psi(\cdot,t)$ has compact support in a fixed compact subset of $\Omega$ and lies in $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, so the spatial distributional equation evaluated at $\psi(\cdot,t)$ gives the identity for the inner integral; integrating over $t$ with [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] (for a compact test supported in $K\times T\Subset\Omega\times I$, each absolute field/density pairing is bounded by $C_\psi\mathbf1_T(t)|F(y)|\mathbf1_K(y)$, whose integral is at most $C_\psi|T|\int_K|F|<\infty$ since $F\in L^1_{\rm loc}$; continuity of $F$ is not required) produces the four-dimensional pairing. For each time-independent component $F$, the time derivative pairing is zero: $\langle\partial_tT_F,\psi\rangle=-\int_K F(y)(\int_I\partial_t\psi(y,t)dt)dy=0$, using the same absolute majorant, Fubini and the fundamental theorem with compact time support. Thus the Faraday and Ampere time terms vanish distributionally. Conversely, testing with $\psi(y,t)=\eta(y)\chi(t)$ for $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, $\chi\in C_c^\infty(I)$ with $\int\chi=1$ recovers the spatial equations, using that all objects are time independent. The point-charge dictionary is the specialisation of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) to the constant trajectory $z\equiv x_0$, which is $C^1$, proper into $U$ (its graph is $\{x_0\}\times I$, whose preimages of compact sets are compact), and whose pairings reduce to $q\int_I\psi(x_0,t)\,dt=\langle q\delta_{x_0},\int_I\psi(\cdot,t)\,dt\rangle$; the spatial point source $q\delta_{x_0}$ is that of [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]. Clause (f) records the frame dependence and the idealization; no boost statement and no dynamics are asserted, so nothing beyond the cited definitions and the two integrations is used. Finite-interval integrations of the continuous one-variable test/radial integrands above use [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]] to identify their Riemann/FTC values with their Lebesgue values before Fubini, polar integration or passage to improper limits; real and imaginary test components are treated separately.

items.title: Scalar potential and the Poisson equation in a star-shaped electrostatic region
items.statement:
Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set that is star-shaped with respect to some $a\in\Omega$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), let $E:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ in the spatial vector-field sense of [[def-em-fields]] ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and let $\rho:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be continuous — the fixed-time reading, in the sense of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], of a pure electrostatic regime with the units and constant $\varepsilon_0>0$ of [[def-em-si-conventions]] ([[def-em-sources]]). Suppose the reduced smooth-branch equations hold pointwise on $\Omega$:
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega,$$
with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Then:
(a) [Closed field and potential] $-E$ is closed in the sense of [[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]] — equivalently $\operatorname{curl}(-E)=0$ ([[cor-curl-vanishes-exactly-when-a-field-is-closed]]) — and the function
$$\varphi(x):=-\int_0^1E\bigl(a+s(x-a)\bigr)\cdot(x-a)\,ds$$
(the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is a $C^2$ function on $\Omega$ with
$$\nabla\varphi=-E\qquad\text{on }\Omega$$
([[thm-poincare-lemma-for-star-shaped-domains]] applied to the closed $C^1$ field $-E$; the integrand and its parameter derivatives are continuous, so the stated potential is $C^2$).
(b) [Poisson equation] with $\Delta\varphi=\operatorname{div}\nabla\varphi$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]],
$$-\Delta\varphi=\operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}\qquad\text{pointwise on }\Omega.$$
(c) [Uniqueness up to constants] if $\psi\in C^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $\nabla\psi=-E$ on $\Omega$, then $\psi-\varphi$ is constant on $\Omega$; in particular $\varphi$ is uniquely determined by $\nabla\varphi=-E$ and one prescribed value. (Star-shapedness gives path-connectedness through the centre $a$, so the constant is the same on all of $\Omega$; [[cor-potentials-differ-by-a-componentwise-constant]], [[def-piecewise-c1-path-connected-conservative-and-path-independent]].)
No normalisation of $\varphi$ at infinity, and no boundary condition, is asserted on a general star-shaped $\Omega$; the additive constant remains free.

items.title: The localized Newtonian potential and the ideal point-charge Coulomb field
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, polar, Newtonian and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Work in $\mathbb R^3$ with its Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]) and the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$. Let $\Phi$ be the $n=3$ fundamental solution of $-\Delta$ of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], normalised by $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$; then $\omega_2=4\pi$ and
$$\Phi(z)=\frac{1}{4\pi|z|}\qquad(z\ne0)$$
([[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]). Let $Nf$ be the Newtonian potential of [[def-newtonian-potential]].
(a) [Smooth compact sources] Let $\rho:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ with compact support contained in $\overline B_R$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-metric-ball]]), put $\varphi:=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho$ and $E:=-\nabla\varphi$. Then $\varphi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ ([[thm-newtonian-potential-for-holder-data-is-classical]]), and pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$
$$-\Delta\varphi=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0$$
with the operators of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Moreover, with $Q:=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ the absolutely convergent Coulomb integral representation holds, and its far-field bound holds for $|x|>2R$,
$$E(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{x-y}{|x-y|^3}\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad |E(x)|\le\frac{\| \rho\|_1}{\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2}\quad(|x|>2R),$$
and for $|x|>\max(2R,1)$ the potential obeys the decay bound $|\varphi(x)|\le\bigl(|Q|/(4\pi)+R\|\rho\|_1/\pi\bigr)/(\varepsilon_0|x|)$ ([[lem-em-newtonian-far-field-gradient]], [[thm-decay-of-the-newtonian-potential-of-compactly-supported-data]]). The pair $(E,0,\rho,0)$ therefore realises the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with source $\rho$, and $E$ is the field of the localised Newtonian potential.
(b) [Uniqueness with vanishing at infinity] If $\psi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfies $-\Delta\psi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$ and $\lim_{|x|\to\infty}\psi(x)=0$, then $\psi=\varphi$ ([[thm-weak-maximum-principle-for-the-laplacian]]). In particular, among $C^2$ solutions of the Poisson equation of a compactly supported $C^1$ source decaying at infinity, the localised Newtonian potential is the unique one.
(c) [Compactly supported $L^1$ sources] If instead $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ is real, measurable and compactly supported, then $N\rho$ is finite $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere, belongs to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, is $C^\infty$ and harmonic off the support of $\rho$, and its regular distribution satisfies
$$-\Delta T_{\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho}=T_{\rho/\varepsilon_0}\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$$
([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]], scaled by $\varepsilon_0^{-1}$; [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]).
(d) [Point charge] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ and $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and define, with arbitrary values at $x_0$,
$$\varphi_q(x):=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|},\qquad E_q(x):=\frac{q\,(x-x_0)}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|^3}\qquad(x\ne x_0).$$
Then $\varphi_q\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $E_q$ is locally integrable and $C^\infty$ off $x_0$, $E_q=-\nabla\varphi_q$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{x_0\}$, and, with $T_{\varphi_q}$ the regular distribution of $\varphi_q$ and $\operatorname{div}E_q:=\sum_i\partial_iT_{E_{q,i}}$, $\operatorname{curl}E_q:=(\partial_2T_{E_{q,3}}-\partial_3T_{E_{q,2}},\ \partial_3T_{E_{q,1}}-\partial_1T_{E_{q,3}},\ \partial_1T_{E_{q,2}}-\partial_2T_{E_{q,1}})$,
$$-\Delta T_{\varphi_q}=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\delta_{x_0},\qquad \operatorname{div}E_q=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\delta_{x_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}E_q=0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$$
([[thm-minus-laplacian-of-the-fundamental-solution-is-dirac]] for the first identity, [[lem-em-distributional-gradient-smooth-off-a-point]] for the passage from the potential to the field, [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]). The distribution $q\delta_{x_0}$ is the fixed-time reading of the stationary point charge of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with charge parameter $q$ and constant trajectory $z\equiv x_0$ ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](e)); so the pair $(E_q,0)$ satisfies the distributional pure electrostatic equations with that point source. This is an idealised point-source model: no claim of uniqueness for the point source, no self-force and no statement about the field at $x_0$ itself is made.
items.strategy:
All uses below inherit the stated $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: Holder regularity, compact $L^1$ distributional Poisson and its Borel-representative construction, the fundamental Dirac identity, decay and the point-field regular-distribution reading. No stronger choice axiom is invoked. Objects and constants: $\Phi$ and its normalisation are those of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]]; $\omega_2=4\pi$ follows from $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$ ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]) and $|B_1|=4\pi/3$ ([[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], $n=3$), giving $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$.
(a) $ho\in C^1_c$ is bounded and Lipschitz: $[ho]_{0,1}=\sup|
ablaho|<\infty$ by compact support, continuity of $
ablaho$ and attainment of the supremum ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]); fix $\alpha=1/2\in(0,1)$; for $|x-y|\le1$ the Holder quotient is at most $\sup|

Scaling $\varphi=\varepsilon_0^{-1}Nho$ and using linearity of the coordinate second derivatives ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives $-\Delta\varphi=ho/\varepsilon_0$; then $\operatorname{div}E=-\Delta\varphi=ho/\varepsilon_0$ because $E=-
abla\varphi$ and $\Delta\varphi=\operatorname{div}

The full first-derivative representation in [[thm-newtonian-potential-for-holder-data-is-classical]] proof steps 2.2–3.1 gives $\partial_iNho(x)=\int\partial_i\Phi(x-y)ho(y)dy$ for every $x$, including inside the support: local integrability of $|z|^{-2}$ in dimension three and bounded compact $ho$ make the integral absolutely convergent, and the cutoff derivative integrals converge uniformly on compact sets to the continuous $G_i$ before the uniform derivative-limit theorem identifies $\partial_iNho$. Thus the displayed Coulomb integral is valid on all $\mathbb R^3$. The far-field bound $|E(x)|\le\|ho\|_1/(\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2)$ are [[lem-em-newtonian-far-field-gradient]] (with $n=3$, $\omega_2=4\pi$, $
abla\Phi(z)=-z/(4\pi|z|^3)$); the potential decay is [[thm-decay-of-the-newtonian-potential-of-compactly-supported-data]] with the same constants, divided by $\varepsilon_0$. The regime reading is [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](c),(d): the displayed pair satisfies the reduced equations with $ho$ and the vanishing time derivatives, since the objects are time independent.
(b) Let $\psi$ be as stated and $h:=\psi-\varphi$; then $h\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ and $\Delta h=0$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], linearity of the second derivatives), while $\lim_{|x|	o\infty}h(x)=0$. Given $\varepsilon>0$ choose $R_\varepsilon$ with $|h|\le\varepsilon$ on $\{|x|\ge R_\varepsilon\}$. For $R>R_\varepsilon$, [[thm-weak-maximum-principle-for-the-laplacian]] applied on the bounded open ball $B_R$ to $h$ (which is $C^2$ on $B_R$ and continuous on $\overline B_R$) gives $\max_{\overline B_R}h=\max_{S_R}h\le\varepsilon$, and applied to $-h$ gives $\min_{\overline B_R}h\ge-\varepsilon$; hence $|h|\le\varepsilon$ on $\overline B_R$. Every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ lies in $B_R$ for $R$ large, so $|h(x)|\le\varepsilon$ for every $x$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, whence $h=0$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]).
(c) $Nho$ finite a.e., locally integrable and class-independent is [[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]]; the identity $-\Delta T_{Nho}=T_{ho}$, scaled by the constant $\varepsilon_0^{-1}$ using linearity of distributional differentiation ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]), gives $-\Delta T_{\varepsilon_0^{-1}Nho}=T_{ho/\varepsilon_0}$; the smoothness and harmonicity off a closed compact set containing the (a.e.) support is the final clause of the same theorem. No differentiability at points of the support is claimed.
(d) $\varphi_q=(q/\varepsilon_0)\Phi(\cdot-x_0)$ by the explicit kernel, hence belongs to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ because $|z|^{-1}$ is locally integrable in $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); $E_q$ equals $-
abla\varphi_q$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{x_0\}$ by the chain rule applied to $|x-x_0|^{-1}$ ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]), and $|
abla\varphi_q|=|q|/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|^2)$ is locally integrable for the same reason. The first distributional identity is [[thm-minus-laplacian-of-the-fundamental-solution-is-dirac]] for the pole $x_0$, scaled by $q/\varepsilon_0$ (linearity of distributional differentiation; [[def-distribution]]). For the field identities, apply [[lem-em-distributional-gradient-smooth-off-a-point]] to $u=\varphi_q$: $u$ is continuous and $C^\infty$ off the single point $x_0$ ([[lem-laplace-fundamental-solution-is-harmonic-off-its-pole]]; the value at the pole is arbitrary and a singleton is null, [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]), and each classical partial $\partial_i\varphi_q$ is locally integrable, so $\partial_iT_{\varphi_q}=T_{\partial_i\varphi_q}$. Since $E_{q,i}=-\partial_i\varphi_q$ everywhere off $x_0$, the functions agree almost everywhere and hence have the same regular distribution ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]], [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]), so $T_{E_{q,i}}=-\partial_iT_{\varphi_q}$. Taking one more distributional derivative ([[def-distributional-derivative]]) and summing over $i$ gives $\operatorname{div}E_q=-\sum_i\partial_i\partial_iT_{\varphi_q}=-\Delta T_{\varphi_q}=(q/\varepsilon_0)\delta_{x_0}$, and pairing mixed derivatives with [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]] ($\partial^\alpha\partial^ eta=\partial^{\alpha+ eta}$) cancels the curl components. items.title: Work of the electrostatic force is the potential difference and is path independent
items.strategy:
The potential exists by [[pthm-em-electrostatic-potential]] with $E=-
abla\varphi$ and $\varphi\in C^2$; in particular $\varphi$ is $C^1$, and $\gamma$ is piecewise $C^1$ with values in the open set $\Omega$, so [[thm-gradient-theorem-for-line-integrals]] applies on every $C^1$ piece: the line integral of $
abla\varphi$ equals the endpoint increment. Applying the vector line integral definitions of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]] to $qE=-q
abla\varphi$, the constant $q$ factors out of the integral and the increments of the pieces telescope at the interior partition points ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]), leaving
$$W(\gamma)=-q\int_\gamma
abla\varphi\cdot d\mathbf r=q\, igl(\varphi(\gamma(t_0))-\varphi(\gamma(t_1)) igr),$$
which is (a). Claim (b) is immediate from (a) because the right-hand side depends only on the endpoints; a closed path has equal endpoints, so its work vanishes. Claim (c) is the definition $U=q\varphi$ and rearrangement, with $q$ in coulombs and $\varphi$ in volts ([[def-em-si-conventions]]). Claim (d): two $C^2$ potentials of the same field differ by a constant on each piecewise-$C^1$ path component ([[cor-potentials-differ-by-a-componentwise-constant]]); a star-shaped $\Omega$ is path-connected through the segments to the centre, so the constant is global and the difference $\varphi(\gamma(t_0))-\varphi(\gamma(t_1))$ is unchanged ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). No dynamics is used: the path is prescribed, the force is the adopted external electric coupling of [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](i), and in the pure electrostatic regime $B=0$ so no magnetic term appears in that coupling ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](b)).

items.title: Finite-source assembly energy equals the electric field energy
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by the Lebesgue, polar and surface interfaces cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\rho\in C^1_c(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ with support in $\overline B_R$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-metric-ball]]), let $\varphi=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho$ and $E=-\nabla\varphi$ be the smooth-branch Coulomb solution of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](a) with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], and let $\Phi$ be the $n=3$ kernel, $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$ ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]). Then:
(a) [Finiteness] the three quantities
$$\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3,\qquad \frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\varphi\,d\lambda_3,\qquad +\frac{1}{2\varepsilon_0}\iint_{\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3}\Phi(x-y)\rho(x)\rho(y)\,d(\lambda_3\times\lambda_3)(x,y)$$
are finite real numbers;
(b) [Identity] they are equal:
$$\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon_0}\iint_{\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3}\Phi(x-y)\rho(x)\rho(y)\,d(\lambda_3\times\lambda_3)(x,y).$$
The last expression is the **external assembly work** of the ideal quasistatic bookkeeping family $\rho_s=s\rho$, $\varphi_s=s\varphi$ for $0\le s\le1$. An added test charge brought from infinity, where the potential is zero, has electric-force work $-dq\,\varphi_s$ by [[pthm-em-electrostatic-work]]; the balancing external work is $+dq\,\varphi_s$. Therefore $W_{\rm ext}=\int_0^1s\,ds\int\rho\varphi=\tfrac12\int\rho\varphi$. Both signs of $\rho$ are allowed. The symmetric double kernel gives the equivalent ordered-pair interpretation of the factor $1/2$.
(c) [Scope] the identity is a statement about the ideal quasi-static assembly of a compactly supported $C^1$ charge distribution in vacuum, all sources being held in place by external support ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]]). It asserts no time-dependent work, no radiation, no material or stability model, and it does not identify the field energy with the rest mass of any particle; the point-source limit is treated separately and is divergent (see the point-charge field energy of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d)).
items.strategy:
The compact continuous source is Borel and the kernel with finite pole assignment is Borel; the double-kernel integrands are therefore Borel/product measurable by [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]], and their Euclidean and product-measure integrals agree by [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]]. Finiteness: $\varphi\in C^2$ and $E\in C^1$ ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](a)); on the bounded set $\overline B_{2R}$ the continuous $|E|^2$ is bounded ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]) and the ball has finite Lebesgue measure, while outside $\{|x|>2R\}$ one has $|E(x)|\le\|ho\|_1/(\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2)$ ([[lem-em-newtonian-far-field-gradient]], [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](a)), so $\int_{|x|>2R}|E|^2\le\|ho\|_1^2/(\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2)\int_{|x|>2R}|x|^{-4}d\lambda_3<\infty$ by the polar formula ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], with $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ from $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$, [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], and $|B_1|=4\pi/3$, [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]) and $\int_{2R}^{\infty}r^{-2}dr<\infty$; the first integral is finite ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). The second integral is finite because $ho$ is bounded with compact support and $\varphi$ is continuous ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]). For the double integral, the integrand is measurable and $\iint|\Phi(x-y)||ho(x)||ho(y)|d\lambda_3d\lambda_3=\int|ho(x)| igl(\int\Phi(x-y)|ho(y)|dy igr)dx$; put $M=\|ho\|_\infty$. Uniformly in $x$, split the inner integral at $|x-y|=1$. On the near part the polar formula and translation invariance give $\int_{|x-y|<1}\Phi(x-y)|ho(y)|dy\le M(4\pi)^{-1}4\pi\int_0^1r\,dr=M/2$; on the far part it is at most $\|ho\|_1/(4\pi)$. Hence the absolute double integral is bounded by $\|ho\|_1(M/2+\|ho\|_1/(4\pi))<\infty$ via [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] and [[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]], with translations preserving measure by [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]. (b) For $R'>R$ consider the ball $B_{R'}$, a bounded $C^1$ domain with outward normal $x/|x|$ on its boundary sphere $S_{R'}$ ([[lem-em-euclidean-balls-and-annuli-are-bounded-c-one-domains]]); Green's first identity [[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] with $u=v=\varphi$ gives
$$\int_{B_{R'}} igl(\varphi\Delta\varphi+|

u\varphi\,dS.$$
Substituting $-\Delta\varphi=ho/\varepsilon_0$ ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](a)) and rearranging,
$$\int_{B_{R'}}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3= rac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{B_{R'}}ho\varphi\,d\lambda_3+\int_{S_{R'}}\varphi\,\partial_
u\varphi\,dS.$$

This gives the first equality of (b); the eventual constancy also identifies the limit with the integral over all of $\mathbb R^3$. For the second equality, insert $\varphi(x)=\varepsilon_0^{-1}\int\Phi(x-y)ho(y)d\lambda_3(y)$ ([[def-newtonian-potential]], [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]]): $\intho\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\varepsilon_0^{-1}\iintho(x)\Phi(x-y)ho(y)\,d\lambda_3(x)d\lambda_3(y)$ by Fubini ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]) applied to the integrable product (finiteness as in (a)); the kernel is symmetric, $\Phi(x-y)=\Phi(y-x)$, so the ordered-pair integral equals twice the unordered-pair sum, which is the displayed factor $	frac12$. The assembly interpretation is external quasistatic bookkeeping with $ho_s=sho$, $\varphi_s=\varepsilon_0^{-1}Nho_s=s\varphi$, and $E_s=sE$. For an infinitesimal charge $dq$ brought from a distant point to $x$, [[pthm-em-electrostatic-work]] gives electric work $dq(\varphi_s({m start})-\varphi_s(x))$, whose infinity limit is $-dq\varphi_s(x)$ by the proved decay. Balancing external work is its negative. With increment $dho_s=ho\,ds$, its integral is $dW_{m ext}=ds\intho(x)\varphi_s(x)dx=s\,ds\intho\varphi$. The absolute finiteness above justifies integration, including signed $ho$; $\int_0^1s\,ds=1/2$ proves the factor. External support holds the source profiles fixed. This family is an accounting prescription, not an asserted time-dependent Maxwell solution, material dynamics, or process without radiation; no particle mass inference follows. items.title: Divergence of the point-charge field energy and the limits of mass inference
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by the Lebesgue and polar interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $q\in\mathbb R$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$, and let $E_q$ be the ideal point-charge field of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d) ([[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]). For $0<\delta<R$ put
$$U_q(\delta,R):=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\{\delta\le|x-x_0|\le R\}}|E_q(x)|^2\,d\lambda_3(x)$$
(the truncated field energy of the shell between the two spheres, [[def-metric-ball]]). Then:
(a) [Exact truncated energy] for all $0<\delta<R$,
$$U_q(\delta,R)=\frac{q^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0}\Bigl(\frac1\delta-\frac1R\Bigr);$$
(b) [Divergence] $\lim_{R\to\infty}U_q(\delta,R)=q^2/(8\pi\varepsilon_0\delta)$ for every $\delta>0$, and for $q\ne0$
$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}U_q(\delta,R)=+\infty\qquad\text{for every }R>0;$$
so the field energy of the ideal point charge is locally infinite at its own location, and any finite-energy treatment of a point-like charge must modify the source/field near the singularity or introduce an explicit cutoff;
(c) [Limits of the mass inference] the identity is a divergence of the *field energy of the idealised point source* in the framework's SI conventions. It does not assert that a physical particle has infinite rest mass, does not identify field energy with rest mass, contains no measurement, and involves neither a self-force nor a contradiction claim for classical electrodynamics: the framework supplies no mass-energy identification for a charged particle, and the smooth compact-source field/assembly energy of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]] remains finite. The compact $L^1$ branch of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] retains its locally integrable potential and distributional Poisson equation; it does not guarantee finite field energy for arbitrary $L^1$ densities. The point source itself is the idealisation of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](e)); its energy divergence is a mathematical property of that idealisation, not an empirical result.
items.strategy:
For (a), $|E_q(x)|=|q|/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|^2)$ for $x\ne x_0$ ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d), [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]), so $|E_q|^2=q^2/(16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2|x-x_0|^4)$ and by the polar formula ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] with the unit-sphere measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ from [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]] and [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]; the integrand is nonnegative and Borel, [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]])
$$\int_{\delta\le|x-x_0|\le R}|E_q|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac{q^2}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2}\cdot 4\pi\int_\delta^R r^{-2}\,dr=\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0^2}\Bigl(\frac1\delta-\frac1R\Bigr),$$
where the one-dimensional integral is evaluated by the fundamental theorem and the derivative of $r\mapsto-1/r$ ([[thm-ftc-second-part]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]); multiplying by $\varepsilon_0/2$ gives (a) ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). For (b), let $R\to\infty$ in (a) for fixed $\delta$ (the left-hand integral increases to the exterior integral by monotone convergence, [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], giving the first limit) and let $\delta\downarrow0$ for fixed $R$: $1/\delta\to\infty$ for $q\ne0$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]] or directly the order properties of the reals), so the truncated energies tend to $+\infty$. Any neighbourhood of $x_0$ therefore contains field energy exceeding any prescribed bound. For (c): the computation uses only the idealised point-source field of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d); it makes no use of, and does not assert, a mass-energy relation for a charged particle, a self-force, a regularisation or any measurement ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]]); the contrast with the finite energies of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]] is the contrast between an extended compactly supported source and the point idealisation. No claims about the field at $x_0$ itself are made: the truncated integrals avoid the singularity ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]). The choice cost is the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of the Lebesgue/polar interface. Finite-interval integrations of the continuous one-variable test/radial integrands above use [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]] to identify their Riemann/FTC values with their Lebesgue values before Fubini, polar integration or passage to improper limits; real and imaginary test components are treated separately.

items.title: The infinite line charge: logarithmic potential, flux normalization and divergent energy
items.strategy:
For (a): on the open set $\Omega$ ([[def-metric-topology]]; $\rho>0$ is the preimage of the open half-line under the continuous $\rho$, [[thm-continuity-preimage-characterisation]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]) the function $\rho$ is smooth — it is the composition of $x\mapsto x_1^2+x_2^2$ with the square root, positive on $\Omega$ ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) — and the chain rule together with the logarithm derivative gives $\nabla\varphi=-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{1}{\rho}\hat e_r=-E$ ([[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).
For (b): with $E_i=\lambda x_i/(2\pi\varepsilon_0\rho^2)$, direct differentiation on $\Omega$ gives $\partial_1E_1+\partial_2E_2=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{(\rho^2-2x_1^2)+(\rho^2-2x_2^2)}{\rho^4}=0$ and $\partial_1E_2-\partial_2E_1=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{-2x_1x_2+2x_1x_2}{\rho^4}=0$; the third components vanish since $E_3=0$ and nothing depends on $x_3$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]). The electrostatic reading is [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (c).
For (c): the displayed map is $C^1$ on an open neighbourhood of the compact Jordan region $D:=[0,2\pi]\times[-L/2,L/2]$; writing $u(\theta)=\operatorname{Re}e^{i\theta}$, $v(\theta)=\operatorname{Im}e^{i\theta}$, the derivative $\frac{d}{d\theta}e^{i\theta}=ie^{i\theta}$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], [[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) gives $\Phi_\theta=(ru',rv',0)=r(-v,u,0)$ and $\Phi_z=(0,0,1)$, so $\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_z=r(u,v,0)\ne0$ on $D^\circ$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); the only seam is $\theta=0\leftrightarrow2\pi$ on the boundary, so $(D,\Phi)$ is an admissible regular surface patch ([[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]], [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]]). Since $E(\Phi(\theta,z))=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}(u,v,0)$ and $u^2+v^2=|e^{i\theta}|^2=1$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]), the flux integrand of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]] is the constant $\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}$, and the patch integral equals $\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\lambda_2(D)=\frac{\lambda L}{\varepsilon_0}$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).
For (d): the superposition identity $E(x)=\lambda\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{x-z e_3}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-z e_3|^3}\,dz$ is verified componentwise: $\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{dt}{(\rho^2+t^2)^{3/2}}=\frac{2}{\rho^2}$ and the third component is odd in $t$ with absolutely convergent integral zero; the whole $z$-integral is absolutely convergent because $\int_{\mathbb R}|x-z e_3|^{-2}dz=\pi/\rho$ and $x\mapsto|D\psi(x)|/\rho(x)$ is integrable for a compactly supported scalar or vector test: a bounding cylinder $\rho\le A$, $|x_3|\le H$ gives $\int 1/\rho\le(2H)2\pi A<\infty$ by transverse polar integration. The same estimate without $D\psi$ proves $E\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R^3)$, and $\int\int|E_{1,z}(x)||D\psi(x)|dzdx\le(4\varepsilon_0)^{-1}\int|D\psi|/\rho<\infty$ proves absolute Fubini integrability. Here $E_{1,z}$ is the translated unit-charge field with the $\varepsilon_0$ normalization of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d); its value on its pole is immaterial ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). The pairing of the $z$-translated unit point-charge field with $\nabla\psi$ is $-\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\psi(0,0,z)$ by [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] (d); substituting into $\langle\operatorname{div}E,\psi\rangle=-\int E\cdot\nabla\psi$ and interchanging by [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] gives $\langle\operatorname{div}E,\psi\rangle=\frac{\lambda}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(0,0,z)\,dz$ for every test function; the curl pairing with every vector test $\Psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ is $\int E\cdot\operatorname{curl}\Psi=\lambda\int dz\int E_{1,z}\cdot\operatorname{curl}\Psi=0$ by that same absolute majorant, since each translated unit-charge field has vanishing distributional curl ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).
For (e): the stated limits of $\varphi$ in $\rho$ and the effect of changing $r_0$ are the elementary properties of the logarithm ([[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]); for the non-star-shapedness witness, given $a\in\Omega$ the point $-a$ lies in $\Omega$ and the segment $s\mapsto a+s(-a)=a(1-2s)$ passes through $0$ at $s=1/2$, which is on the excluded axis ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]).
For (f): $|E|^2=\frac{\lambda^2}{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2\rho^2}$, and the polar formula in the two transverse coordinates ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], $\sigma(S^1)=2\pi$ from $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$ with $|B_1|=\pi$ in the plane, [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]) gives $\int_{\delta<\rho<R}\rho^{-2}\,d\lambda_2=2\pi\log(R/\delta)$; multiplying by the height $L$ and by $\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\cdot\frac{\lambda^2}{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2}$ yields the displayed identity, and $\log(R/\delta)\to\infty$ in either limit ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] for the monotone convergence of the truncated integrals).
Clause (g) records the scope: [[def-em-weak-sources]] declares only point and stationary-sheet sources, so $\rho_\lambda$ is outside the framework's source types and the item makes no physical, equilibrium or empirical claim. For $\lambda=0$, both $E$ and $\varphi$ and $\rho_\lambda$ are zero, all fluxes and cutoff energies vanish, and the infinity normalization is available; the failure of that normalization and the two energy divergences concern only $\lambda\ne0$. The axis is null (a transverse singleton times bounded longitudinal intervals), so the zero extension does not alter regular distributions. The line-source functional is a distribution because on each compact test support its absolute pairing is at most $|\lambda|(2H)\|\psi\|_\infty$. The axis is contained in the coordinate hyperplane $x_1=0$, which is null by [[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]]. The translated unit-point field, with zero value at its pole, is jointly Borel in $(x,z)$; the scalar/vector-test products are Borel, and [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]] with [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] supplies the product-measure identification for these Fubini calculations. The longitudinal integrals in (d) are evaluated first on finite intervals by [[thm-ftc-second-part]] and [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]: $t/(\rho^2\sqrt{\rho^2+t^2})$ is a primitive of $(\rho^2+t^2)^{-3/2}$, with limiting values $\pm1/\rho^2$; the third component is odd. Absolute convergence then passes to the full line. For the exact absolute-kernel majorant, evenness and the monotone substitution $t=\rho\sqrt{u/(1-u)}$ on $0<u<1$ give $\int_{\mathbb R}(\rho^2+t^2)^{-1}dt=\rho^{-1}B(1/2,1/2)=\pi/\rho$. The substitution has positive continuous derivative on compact truncations; [[thm-substitution-for-improper-integrals]] applies, with Riemann/Lebesgue comparison on those truncations and monotone convergence at the endpoints. The value follows from [[def-real-beta-integral]], [[thm-real-beta-gamma-identity]], [[cor-real-gamma-one-half-is-root-pi]] and $\Gamma(1)=1$ in [[thm-real-gamma-functional-equation]].

items.title: The uniformly charged ball: interior and exterior fields, continuous potential and finite energy
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, polar, Newtonian and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $a>0$, $Q\in\mathbb R$, let $\overline B_a=\{x:|x|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), and define, with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] ([[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]]),
$$\rho(x):=\frac{3Q}{4\pi a^3}\,\mathbf 1_{\{|x|<a\}}(x),\qquad
E(x):=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\begin{cases}x/a^3,&|x|<a,\\ x/|x|^3,&|x|\ge a,\end{cases}\qquad
\varphi(x):=\begin{cases}\dfrac{Q(3a^2-|x|^2)}{8\pi\varepsilon_0a^3},&|x|\le a,\\[6pt]\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|},&|x|\ge a.\end{cases}$$
(The value of $\rho$ on the sphere $\{|x|=a\}$ is immaterial: it is a Lebesgue-null set by the polar calculation $\lambda_3(S_a)=4\pi\int_0^\infty\mathbf1_{\{a\}}(r)r^2dr=0$, since the one-dimensional singleton has measure zero ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]).) Then:
(a) [Regularity and gradient] $E$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^3$, of class $C^\infty$ on each of the open regions $\{|x|<a\}$, $\{|x|>a\}$; $\varphi\in C^1(\mathbb R^3)$, its displayed branch derivatives agree on $\{|x|=a\}$, and $E=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]);
(b) [Classical equations] for every $x$ with $|x|\ne a$,
$$\operatorname{div}E(x)=\rho(x)/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E(x)=0$$
([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]);
(c) [Weak equations] the pair $(E,(\rho,0))$ satisfies the spatial distributional equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$: $E$ is $C^1$ on each side of the sphere $S_a=\{|x|=a\}$ with one-sided continuous traces that agree, $[E]=0$, so [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] gives
$$\operatorname{div}E=\{\operatorname{div}E\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\cdot[E]\,\delta_{S_a}=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=\{\operatorname{curl}E\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[E]\,\delta_{S_a}=0,$$
with $\rho$ the displayed locally integrable density and no surface-charge term ([[def-em-weak-sources]], [[lem-em-euclidean-balls-and-annuli-are-bounded-c-one-domains]] for the sphere as a compact embedded smooth hypersurface); by the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e) these are the weak equations of the static model for this source, with zero singular part;
(d) [Energy] the field energy is finite and equals the assembly integral,
$$\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\frac{3Q^2}{20\pi\varepsilon_0a},$$
computed with the polar formula ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]); the value agrees with the smooth-source identity of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]] although the density here is only piecewise continuous;
(e) [Consistency and contrast] for $|x|>a$ the field is exactly the point-charge Coulomb field of total charge $Q$ centred at the origin ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] (d) with $x_0=0$) although the source is the extended ball, and for $|x|<a$ it is the affine field $Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3)$; $\varphi$ is continuous at $|x|=a$ and decays at infinity; the field is bounded on $\mathbb R^3$, so no divergence of field energy occurs for the extended source;
(f) [Scope] the example verifies the displayed candidate and its energy; it does not claim uniqueness of the solution (this would require boundary data and an infinity condition, and the density is not continuous), it asserts no empirical content, and the density $\rho$ is treated as a bounded $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ density with the sphere carrying no surface charge ($[E]=0$).
items.strategy:
For (a): on $\{|x|<a\}$, $E$ is the affine map $Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3)$ and on $\{|x|>a\}$ it is $Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^3)$; both are $C^\infty$ on their open domains ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]). At $|x|=a$ the two formulas coincide ($x/a^3=x/a^3$), so $E$ is continuous on all of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[def-metric-ball]]). For $\varphi$, the interior branch has gradient $-Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3)$ and the exterior branch has gradient $-Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^3)$ by the chain rule, and the two gradients agree on $\{|x|=a\}$; the matching derivatives also exist on the interface, as follows. Let $F(r)$ be the displayed radial potential profile on $r\ge0$. Its two branches agree at $a$, and their one-sided derivatives both equal $-Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^2)$, so the difference quotient $(F(a+h)-F(a))/h$ has that common limit from either sign. Thus $F$ is differentiable at $a$, and its derivative is continuous there by the branch formulas. Since $x\mapsto|x|$ is differentiable near each point of $S_a$, the chain rule proves actual total differentiability of $\varphi=F(|x|)$ there and gives the matching gradient. At the origin the interior polynomial already gives smoothness. The resulting partial derivatives exist and are continuous everywhere, whence $\varphi$ is $C^1$ with $\nabla\varphi=-E$ ([[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
For (b): inside, $\operatorname{div}(Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3))=3Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3)=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and the curl of an affine field vanishes ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]); outside, $\operatorname{div}(Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^3))=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\sum_i\partial_i(x_i|x|^{-3})=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}(3|x|^{-3}-3|x|^{-3})=0$ and the curl components $\partial_j(x_k|x|^{-3})-\partial_k(x_j|x|^{-3})=0$ vanish by the same direct differentiation ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]), matching $\rho=0$ outside.
For (c): the set $S_a$ is a compact embedded smooth hypersurface with unit normal $n=x/|x|$, and the two sides $\Omega_-=\{|x|<a\}$, $\Omega_+=\{|x|>a\}$ are open; $E$ is $C^1$ on each side and its one-sided traces agree on $S_a$ (from (a)), so $[E]=F_+-F_-=0$ in the notation of [[def-em-surface-distribution]] and [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] applies: the distributional divergence is the piecewise classical divergence plus $n\cdot[E]\delta_{S_a}=0$, and the distributional curl is the piecewise classical curl plus $n\times[E]\delta_{S_a}=0$. By (b) the piecewise divergence is $\rho/\varepsilon_0$ as a locally integrable function and the piecewise curl is $0$; the sphere is null by applying [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] to its Borel indicator: $\lambda_3(S_a)=4\pi\int_0^\infty\mathbf1_{\{a\}}(r)r^2dr=0$. A singleton is contained in intervals of arbitrarily small length, so its one-dimensional measure is zero; [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]] then applies, and the pairing conventions are those of [[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. The static reading is [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e), and the source objects are those of [[def-em-weak-sources]] with zero singular part.
For (d): by the polar formula and $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]) one has $\int_{B_a}|x|^2\,d\lambda_3=4\pi\int_0^ar^4\,dr=\frac{4\pi a^5}{5}$ and $\int_{B_a}d\lambda_3=\frac{4\pi a^3}{3}$; hence
$$\int_{B_a}|E|^2=\Bigl(\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3}\Bigr)^2\frac{4\pi a^5}{5}=\frac{Q^2}{20\pi\varepsilon_0^2a},\qquad \int_{|x|>a}|E|^2=\frac{Q^2}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2}\cdot 4\pi\int_a^\infty r^{-2}dr=\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0^2a},$$
using $\int_a^\infty r^{-2}dr=1/a$ ([[thm-ftc-second-part]] and monotone convergence, [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); the sum times $\varepsilon_0/2$ is $\frac{Q^2}{40\pi\varepsilon_0a}+\frac{Q^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0a}=\frac{3Q^2}{20\pi\varepsilon_0a}$. The assembly integral is computed from the same two radial integrals, $\frac12\int\rho\varphi=\frac12\frac{3Q}{4\pi a^3}\frac{Q}{8\pi\varepsilon_0a^3}\bigl(3a^2\frac{4\pi a^3}{3}-\frac{4\pi a^5}{5}\bigr)=\frac{3Q^2}{20\pi\varepsilon_0a}$, so the identity of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]] extends to this piecewise-continuous bounded density by direct verification; the density is bounded with compact support and all integrands are continuous off a null sphere ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]).
For (e): the exterior branch equals the formula of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] (d) with $q=Q$, $x_0=0$; $\varphi$ is continuous at $|x|=a$ since both branches give $Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a)$, and decays like $1/|x|$; $|E|\le |Q|/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^2)$ on $\mathbb R^3$, so the energy of (d) is finite and no point singularity arises. For (f): no uniqueness or empirical statement is used anywhere; the sphere's zero jump is exactly the checked equality of the two branches on $\{|x|=a\}$. The one-dimensional singleton used in the polar null-sphere calculation is null by [[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]]. Finite-interval integrations of the continuous one-variable test/radial integrands above use [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]] to identify their Riemann/FTC values with their Lebesgue values before Fubini, polar integration or passage to improper limits; real and imaginary test components are treated separately.
